title_en: The simple past of sein and haben

rule.summary: For most verbs, spoken German uses the Perfekt for the past. **sein** and **haben** are different: people almost always use the **Präteritum** (*war, hatte*), even in conversation. The same is true for the modal verbs (*konnte, musste, wollte*) and *wissen* (*wusste*). The Präteritum is one word in position 2, so there is no Satzklammer: *Ich war krank. Wir hatten keine Zeit.*
rule.table:
| Person | sein | haben | können (Modalverb) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | war | hatte | konnte |
| du | war**st** | hatte**st** | konnte**st** |
| er / sie / es | war | hatte | konnte |
| wir | war**en** | hatte**n** | konnte**n** |
| ihr | war**t** | hatte**t** | konnte**t** |
| sie / Sie | war**en** | hatte**n** | konnte**n** |
steps: Use the Präteritum of *sein* and *haben* for the past in speech and writing: *Ich war zu Hause* is more common than *Ich bin zu Hause gewesen*.
Take the stem: *sein → war-*, *haben → hatte-* (the *b* is replaced by *t*, plus the past marker *-te*).
Add the personal ending: *ich* and *er/sie/es* have **no ending** (*ich war, er hatte*); *du* **-st**, *wir/sie/Sie* **-(e)n**, *ihr* **-t**.
Put the verb in position 2 (position 1 in yes/no questions). Nothing goes to the end, because there is no participle.
Remember expressions with *haben* where English uses *be*: *Hunger/Durst/Angst haben, recht haben, Glück haben, Geburtstag haben*.
pitfalls: Adding an ending for *ich* or *er*: ✗ *Ich hattete keine Zeit.* → ✓ *Ich hatte keine Zeit.* The *-te* is already the past marker.
Using *sein* where German uses *haben*: ✗ *Ich war Hunger.* → ✓ *Ich hatte Hunger.* (English: *I was hungry.*)
Mixing up the *ihr*-forms: ✓ *ihr wart* (from *sein*), ✓ *ihr hattet* (from *haben*); *ihr wartet* is the verb *warten* (to wait).
Confusing the Präteritum with the Konjunktiv II: *ich war* (I was) but *ich wäre* (I would be); *ich hatte* (I had) but *ich hätte* (I would have).
Wrong person ending: ✗ *Du war müde.* → ✓ *Du warst müde.* ✗ *Wir war …* → ✓ *Wir waren …*

items.explanation: *gestern* shows the past, and with *sein* German uses the Präteritum. The *ich*-form has no ending: **war**. *müde* is a predicative adjective and has no ending.

mistake.why: *waren* is the form for *wir* and *sie/Sie*. For *ich* the Präteritum of *sein* has no ending: *ich war*.

examples.de: Ich war am Montag beim Zahnarzt.
examples.en: I was at the dentist's on Monday.
I was very nervous.

items.de: Du {{c1::warst::sein}} den ganzen Tag zu Hause.
items.en: You were at home all day.
items.explanation: The *du*-form adds **-st** to the stem *war-*: **warst**. *den ganzen Tag* is an Akkusativ of time.

mistake.wrong: Du war den ganzen Tag zu Hause.
mistake.why: *war* without ending is only for *ich* and *er/sie/es*. The *du*-form always ends in *-st*: *du warst*.

examples.de: Du warst gestern nicht im Kurs.
examples.en: You weren't in class yesterday.
You were very brave.

items.explanation: *er/sie/es* has the same form as *ich*, without any ending: **war**. *in der Schule* is a location (Dativ, *wo?*).

mistake.why: *wart* is the *ihr*-form. For *er* the form is *war* with no ending.

examples.en: She was in the library.
He was at the hairdresser's.

items.en: We were at the cinema yesterday.
items.explanation: *wir* adds **-en** to the stem *war-*: **waren**. In speech *Wir waren im Kino* is the normal way to say this; *Wir sind im Kino gewesen* is possible but less common.

mistake.why: *wart* belongs to *ihr*. The *wir*-form ends in *-en*: *wir waren*.

examples.de: Wir waren am Samstag im Theater.
examples.en: We were at the theatre on Saturday.

examples.de: Wir waren letzte Woche in Prag.
examples.en: We were in Prague last week.

items.en: You (pl.) were very nice to me.
items.explanation: The *ihr*-form adds only **-t** to *war-*: **wart**, without an *-e-*. *nett zu* + Dativ: *zu mir*.

mistake.wrong: Ihr wartet sehr nett zu mir.
mistake.why: *wartet* is the present tense of *warten* (to wait). The Präteritum of *sein* for *ihr* is *wart*.

examples.de: Ihr wart sehr freundlich zu uns.
examples.en: You (pl.) were very friendly to us.
You (pl.) were very funny yesterday.

items.en: They were on holiday in Spain.
items.explanation: *sie* (they) takes the same ending as *wir*: **waren**. A location (*in Spanien*) needs *sein*, not *haben*.

mistake.wrong: Sie hatten im Urlaub in Spanien.
mistake.why: To say where someone was, German uses *sein*. *haben* needs an object: *Sie hatten Urlaub.*

examples.de: Sie waren eine Woche in Griechenland.
examples.en: They were in Greece for a week.

examples.de: Meine Eltern waren im Sommer an der Ostsee.
examples.en: My parents were at the Baltic Sea in the summer.

items.explanation: The past stem of *haben* is *hatte-*: the *b* becomes *t* and the past marker *-te* follows. The *ich*-form has no extra ending: **hatte**.

mistake.why: *hatte* already contains the past marker *-te*. Adding another *-te* is wrong: *ich hatte*.

examples.en: I wasn't hungry.

examples.de: Ich hatte einen Termin beim Arzt.
examples.en: I had a doctor's appointment.

items.en: You had a very good idea.
items.explanation: *du* adds **-st** to the past stem *hatte-*: **hattest**. The Akkusativ object *eine sehr gute Idee* follows.

mistake.wrong: Du hatte eine sehr gute Idee.
mistake.why: The *du*-form always needs *-st*: *du hattest*.

examples.en: You had a hard week.
You had visitors yesterday.

items.explanation: German says *Hunger haben* where English says *be hungry*, so the verb is *haben*. *sie* (she) has the same form as *ich*: **hatte**.

mistake.why: *Hunger* is a noun object of *haben*. *sein* cannot take this object: *Sie hatte Hunger.*

examples.en: He was very thirsty.
The child had a temperature.

items.de: Wir {{c1::hatten::haben}} viel Spaß auf der Party.
items.en: We had a lot of fun at the party.
items.explanation: *wir* adds **-n** to *hatte-*: **hatten**. *Spaß haben* = to have fun.

mistake.wrong: Wir hattet viel Spaß auf der Party.
mistake.why: *hattet* is the *ihr*-form. For *wir* the form is *hatten*.

examples.en: We had a lot of work.

examples.de: Wir hatten schönes Wetter im Urlaub.
examples.en: We had nice weather on holiday.

items.de: {{c1::Hattet::haben}} ihr ein Problem mit dem Auto?
items.en: Did you (pl.) have a problem with the car?
items.explanation: The *ihr*-form adds **-t** to *hatte-*: **hattet**. In a yes/no question the verb is in position 1.

mistake.wrong: Hatten ihr ein Problem mit dem Auto?
mistake.why: *hatten* is for *wir* and *sie/Sie*. With *ihr* the ending is *-t*: *Hattet ihr …?*

examples.de: Hattet ihr eine gute Zeit in Wien?
examples.en: Did you (pl.) have a good time in Vienna?

examples.de: Hattet ihr Probleme mit dem Hotel?
examples.en: Did you (pl.) have problems with the hotel?

items.en: They didn't have a dog back then.
items.explanation: *sie* (they) takes **-n**: **hatten**. *damals* (back then) refers to a period in the past, which fits the Präteritum well.

mistake.why: *haben* is irregular in the Präteritum: the stem is *hatte-*, not *habte-*.

examples.en: They had little money back then.

examples.de: Meine Großeltern hatten einen großen Garten.
examples.en: My grandparents had a big garden.

items.en: We were young at that time.
items.explanation: *damals* refers to a past period. For *wir* the form is **waren** (stem *war-* + *-en*).

mistake.why: *war* has no ending and fits only *ich* and *er/sie/es*. *wir* needs *-en*: *wir waren*.

examples.en: We were students at that time.
We were very happy at that time.

items.en: She didn't have a key with her.
items.explanation: *dabeihaben* is separable. In the Präteritum the verb part *hatte* stands in position 2 and *dabei* goes to the end. *sie* (she) → **hatte** without ending.

mistake.why: *hattet* is the *ihr*-form. For *sie* (she) the form is *hatte*.

examples.en: He didn't have any ID with him.
I didn't have any money on me.

items.explanation: *du* → stem *war-* + *-st* → **warst**. The adjective *leise* is predicative and has no ending.

mistake.why: *wart* is the *ihr*-form (*-t*). The *du*-form ends in *-st*: *du warst*.

examples.en: You were very patient.
You were very hard-working today.

items.explanation: *Angst haben* = to be afraid; German uses *haben* + the noun *Angst*. *ich* → **hatte**. *große Angst* is the Akkusativ object (feminine, adjective *-e*).

mistake.why: English uses *be*, but German uses *haben* with the noun *Angst*: *Ich hatte Angst.*

examples.en: He was very worried.
I had a headache.

items.explanation: *er* → **war** without ending. *nicht* follows the verb and negates the place *zu Hause*.

mistake.why: *waren* is plural. The subject *er* is singular: *er war*.

examples.en: She was not in the office.

examples.de: Der Chef war heute nicht da.
examples.en: The boss wasn't there today.

items.explanation: *wir* → *hatte-* + *-n* → **hatten**. The ending depends on the subject *wir*, not on the plural object *viele Freunde*.

mistake.why: *hatte* is for *ich* and *er/sie/es*. With *wir* the verb needs *-n*: *wir hatten*.

examples.en: We had two cats.
We had a lot of guests.

items.explanation: In a yes/no question the verb comes first. *ihr* → *war-* + *-t* → **Wart**.

mistake.why: *waren* is for *wir* and *sie/Sie*. With *ihr* the form is *wart*.

examples.en: Have you (pl.) been to the museum yet?

examples.de: Wart ihr gestern auf dem Markt?
examples.en: Were you (pl.) at the market yesterday?

items.explanation: An adjective that describes the subject (*froh*) needs *sein*. *sie* (they) → **waren**.

mistake.why: *haben* needs an object. To describe how someone was, use *sein*: *Sie waren froh.*

examples.en: The guests were very satisfied.
They were very surprised.

items.explanation: With *sein* speakers prefer the Präteritum even in conversation: **war**, not *bin … gewesen*. The *ich*-form has no ending.

mistake.why: *warst* is the *du*-form. For *ich* the form is *war* without ending.

examples.en: I was at the office yesterday.

examples.de: Ich war am Wochenende bei meinen Eltern.
examples.en: I was at my parents' place at the weekend.

items.en: Have you ever been to Italy?
items.explanation: The formal *Sie* takes the same form as *wir*: **Waren** Sie …? German uses the Präteritum of *sein* here, where English uses the present perfect (*have you ever been*).

mistake.wrong: Wart Sie schon einmal in Italien?
mistake.why: *wart* is the *ihr*-form. Formal *Sie* takes *waren*.

examples.de: Waren Sie schon einmal in Berlin?
examples.en: Have you ever been to Berlin?
Were you at the office yesterday?

items.explanation: *haben* forms its past stem irregularly: the *b* is replaced by *t* and *-te* is added → *hatte-*. For *wir* + *-n*: **hatten**.

mistake.why: *hattet* has the *ihr*-ending *-t*. For *wir* the form is *hatten*.

examples.en: We had no chance.
We didn't feel like it.

items.explanation: Modal verbs also prefer the Präteritum. *können* drops the umlaut and adds *-te*: **konnte**. The infinitive *schlafen* goes to the end.

mistake.why: *kannte* is the Präteritum of *kennen* (to know a person). The Präteritum of *können* is *konnte*.

examples.en: She could swim well.
I couldn't call you.

items.explanation: *müssen* loses the umlaut and adds *-te*: **musste** (with *ss*). For *sie* (she) there is no extra ending. This is much more common than the Perfekt *hat gehen müssen*.

mistake.why: *musstet* is the *ihr*-form. For *sie* (she) the form is *musste*.

examples.en: I had to wait a long time.
He had to work on Saturday.

items.en: I didn't want to disturb you.
items.explanation: *wollen* has no umlaut to lose; the Präteritum is the stem *woll-* + *-te*: **wollte**. *Ich wollte nicht stören* is a common polite phrase.

mistake.why: The vowel *i* belongs only to the present singular (*ich will*). The Präteritum uses *o*: *wollte*.

examples.en: I just wanted to ask quickly.
We wanted to go to the cinema.

items.explanation: Weather is described with the impersonal subject *es* + *sein*. *es* takes the form without ending: **war**.

mistake.why: *es* is singular, so the verb has no plural ending: *es war*.

examples.en: It was very hot.
It was foggy yesterday.

items.en: Did you have a car back then?
items.explanation: *du* adds *-st* after the past marker *-te*: hat + te + st → **hattest**. In the yes/no question the verb is in position 1.

mistake.why: The *du*-form needs the ending *-st*: *Hattest du …?*

examples.en: Did you have a nice holiday?
Did you have time yesterday?

items.en: We weren't allowed to take photos.
items.explanation: *dürfen* loses the umlaut and adds *-te*: *durfte-*. For *wir* + *-n*: **durften**. Do not keep the umlaut: *dürften* is the Konjunktiv II (*might*).

mistake.why: The past marker *-te-* is missing. The Präteritum is *durften*.

examples.en: We were allowed to stay up late.
The children were allowed to play outside.

items.explanation: *ihr* + *war-* + *-t* → **wart**, with no *-e-* in between (compare *ihr hattet*, where *-te-* already contains an *e*).

mistake.why: No *-e-* is inserted after *war-*: the *ihr*-form is short, *wart*. *waret* is not a modern standard form.

examples.en: You (pl.) were very punctual.
You (pl.) were really great.

items.explanation: *Hunger haben* keeps *haben* in every tense: *ich habe Hunger → ich **hatte** Hunger*. *großen Hunger* is a masculine Akkusativ object.

mistake.why: *hattest* is the *du*-form. For *ich* the form is *hatte* without ending.

examples.en: I was very thirsty.
My feet were cold.

items.en: They were actually supposed to come at eight.
items.explanation: *sollen* → *sollte-* (no umlaut, so nothing changes in the stem) + *-n* for *sie* (they) → **sollten**. With *eigentlich* it often describes a plan that did not happen.

mistake.wrong: Sie solltet eigentlich um acht kommen.
mistake.why: *solltet* is the *ihr*-form. For *sie* (they) the ending is *-n*: *sollten*.

examples.de: Wir sollten eigentlich um neun da sein.
examples.en: We were actually supposed to be there at nine.
He was actually supposed to call today.

items.explanation: *das* refers to one thing → **war** (singular). After *sein* the noun is a Nominativ: *eine gute Entscheidung*.

mistake.why: *waren* is used only when the noun after *das* is plural (*Das waren gute Tage*). With one decision the verb is singular: *war*.

examples.en: That was a great trip.
That was a lovely evening.

items.en: We didn't have internet back then.
items.explanation: *damals* marks a past period; with *haben* the Präteritum is natural: **hatten** (*wir* → *-n*). *kein Internet* negates the noun.

mistake.why: *hat* is the present tense for *er/sie/es*. The subject is *wir* and the time is past: *wir hatten*.

examples.en: We didn't have a TV back then.
We didn't have mobile phones back then.

items.explanation: *mögen* has a special past stem: *ö → o* and *g → ch*: *mochte-*. *er* takes no ending: **mochte**.

mistake.why: The Präteritum of *mögen* changes the stem to *moch-*: *mochte*. (*möchte* without *-g-* is the Konjunktiv II: *would like*.)

examples.en: She didn't like the film.
I liked my teacher very much.

items.explanation: *wissen* behaves like a modal verb: the stem changes *i → u* and *-te* is added: **wusste**. Like *war* and *hatte*, it is used in the Präteritum even in speech.

mistake.why: The Präteritum of *wissen* has the vowel *u*: *wusste*.

examples.en: He knew the answer.
We didn't know anything about it.

items.en: Where were you at the weekend?
items.explanation: In a W-question the verb is in position 2, after the question word. *du* → *war-* + *-st* → **warst**. This is the normal way to ask where someone was.

mistake.why: *wart* is the *ihr*-form. With *du* the ending is *-st*: *Wo warst du?*

examples.en: Where were you last night?

examples.de: Wie lange warst du in Paris?
examples.en: How long were you in Paris?

items.explanation: German says *Geburtstag haben* (English: *it is my birthday*). *Gestern* is in position 1, so the verb **hatte** is in position 2 and *ich* follows it.

mistake.why: *Geburtstag* is the object of *haben*, not a description of the person: *Ich hatte Geburtstag.*

examples.de: Letzte Woche hatte meine Mutter Geburtstag.
examples.en: It was my mother's birthday last week.

examples.de: Am Montag hatte ich keinen Unterricht.
examples.en: I had no lessons on Monday.

items.explanation: *recht haben* = to be right; German uses *haben*, not *sein*. *du* → *hatte-* + *-st* → **hattest**. *recht* is normally written in lower case in this phrase (*Recht haben* is also allowed).

mistake.why: English says *you were right*, but the German phrase is *recht haben*: *Du hattest recht.*

examples.en: She was right.
You (pl.) were right.

items.en: What was the weather like in London?
items.explanation: The subject *das Wetter* is singular (3rd person), so the verb is **war**. *Wie war …?* is the standard question about an experience in the past.

mistake.wrong: Wie waren das Wetter in London?
mistake.why: *das Wetter* is singular, so the verb has no plural ending: *Wie war das Wetter?*

examples.en: How was the exam?
How was your holiday?

items.en: Did you have a good trip?
items.explanation: Formal *Sie* takes the same form as *wir* and *sie* (they): *hatte-* + *-n* → **Hatten**. The verb comes first in a yes/no question.

mistake.why: *hattet* is for *ihr*. Formal *Sie* always takes the plural form: *Hatten Sie …?*

examples.en: Did you have an appointment?
Did you have a nice evening?

items.en: He had a temperature and was in bed.
items.explanation: c1: *Fieber* is an Akkusativ object → *haben*: **hatte**. c2: *im Bett* is a location → *sein*: **war**. Both verbs share the subject *er*, so both have no ending.
items.pattern: er + hatte + Objekt + und + war + Ort

mistake.wrong: Er hatte Fieber und hatte im Bett.
mistake.why: A location needs *sein*: *war im Bett*. *haben* would need an object.

examples.de: Sie hatte Husten und war zu Hause.
examples.en: She had a cough and was at home.

examples.de: Wir hatten Zeit und waren im Park.
examples.en: We had time and were in the park.

items.focus: Präteritum von haben · Nomen als Subjekt
items.explanation: The subject *mein Handy* is a singular noun (3rd person) → **hatte** without ending. *kein … mehr* = no more.

mistake.wrong: Mein Handy hatten keinen Akku mehr.
mistake.why: *mein Handy* is singular, so the verb has no plural *-n*: *hatte*.

examples.en: The hotel had no car park.

examples.de: Der Zug hatte eine Stunde Verspätung.
examples.en: The train was an hour late.

items.de: Letztes Jahr {{c1::war::sein}} ich drei Wochen in Portugal.
items.en: Last year I was in Portugal for three weeks.
items.explanation: *Letztes Jahr* takes position 1, so the verb **war** comes in position 2 and the subject *ich* after it. *drei Wochen* is a duration (Akkusativ).

mistake.wrong: Letztes Jahr ich war drei Wochen in Portugal.
mistake.why: The verb must be in position 2. After a time phrase in position 1, the subject comes after the verb: *Letztes Jahr war ich …*

examples.de: Im Sommer war ich zwei Wochen in Norwegen.
examples.en: In the summer I was in Norway for two weeks.

examples.de: Am Dienstag war sie in Basel.
examples.en: On Tuesday she was in Basel.

items.explanation: *können* → *konnte-* (umlaut gone) + *-st* for *du* → **Konntest**. In the question the modal is in position 1 and the infinitive *kommen* at the end.

mistake.why: Modal verbs follow the same endings as *hatte*: *du* needs *-st*: *Konntest du …?*

examples.en: Did you have to wait long?
Didn't you want to come along?

items.en: Back then, rents were still cheap.
items.explanation: The subject *die Mieten* is plural, so the verb is **waren**, even though the subject comes after it (inversion after *Damals*).

mistake.wrong: Damals war die Mieten noch billig.
mistake.why: The verb agrees with the subject, not with the word in position 1. *die Mieten* is plural → *waren*.

examples.en: Back then the streets were empty.
The winters used to be colder.

items.explanation: *ihr* → *hatte-* + *-t* → **hattet**. The question word *warum* is in position 1 and the verb in position 2.

mistake.why: *hattest* is the *du*-form. With *ihr* the ending is *-t*: *hattet*.

examples.en: When were you (pl.) on holiday?
Why didn't you (pl.) have a ticket?

items.de: Wir {{c1::waren::sein}} in Rom und haben viel gesehen.
items.en: We were in Rome and saw a lot.
items.explanation: In everyday speech people combine both tenses: *sein* in the Präteritum (**waren**), other verbs in the Perfekt (*haben … gesehen*). *in Rom* is a location → *sein*.

mistake.wrong: Wir hatten in Rom und haben viel gesehen.
mistake.why: A place where someone was needs *sein*: *Wir waren in Rom.* *haben* would need an object.

examples.de: Ich war beim Arzt und habe ein Rezept bekommen.
examples.en: I was at the doctor's and got a prescription.

examples.de: Wir hatten Hunger und haben Pizza bestellt.
examples.en: We were hungry and ordered pizza.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about the use of the Präteritum.
drills.prompt: Why do Germans say *Ich war krank* rather than *Ich bin krank gewesen* in conversation?
drills.answer: For **sein**, **haben**, the **modal verbs** and **wissen**, the Präteritum is the normal past tense, also in speech. Most other verbs use the Perfekt in speech.
drills.explanation: The Perfekt of *sein* and *haben* is correct but sounds long and heavy (*bin gewesen, habe gehabt*). So a typical spoken sentence mixes tenses: *Ich war müde und bin früh ins Bett gegangen.*

examples.en: I was ill yesterday.

examples.de: Ich war müde und bin früh ins Bett gegangen.
examples.en: I was tired and went to bed early.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about the endings.
drills.prompt: Which persons have no ending in the Präteritum, and what are the other endings?
drills.answer: **ich** and **er/sie/es** have no ending (*war, hatte*). *du* **-st**, *wir* and *sie/Sie* **-(e)n**, *ihr* **-t**: *warst, waren, wart / hattest, hatten, hattet*.
drills.explanation: This is different from the present tense, where *ich* has *-e* and *er* has *-t*. In the Präteritum *ich* and *er* always look the same, for every verb (*ich konnte – er konnte*).

examples.en: I was in the garden.
He was in the garden too.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about *haben* in fixed expressions.
drills.prompt: Which common expressions use *haben* in German where English uses *to be*?
drills.answer: **Hunger/Durst haben** (be hungry/thirsty), **Angst haben** (be afraid), **recht haben** (be right), **Glück haben** (be lucky), **Geburtstag haben** (it is someone's birthday), **Verspätung haben** (be late – trains, buses).
drills.explanation: In these expressions the second word is a noun object of *haben*, so *sein* is not possible. In the past they all use *hatte*: *Wir hatten Glück.*

examples.de: Wir hatten Glück mit dem Wetter.
examples.en: We were lucky with the weather.

examples.de: Der Bus hatte zehn Minuten Verspätung.
examples.en: The bus was ten minutes late.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about similar-looking forms.
drills.prompt: What is the difference between *ihr wart*, *ihr hattet* and *ihr wartet*?
drills.answer: **ihr wart** = you were (Präteritum of *sein*). **ihr hattet** = you had (Präteritum of *haben*). **ihr wartet** = you wait (present tense of *warten*).
drills.explanation: *sein* adds only *-t* (*wart*), but *haben* already has the past marker *-te* and then adds *-t* (*hattet*). *wartet* has nothing to do with *sein*.

examples.en: You (pl.) weren't there yesterday.
You (pl.) have been waiting a long time, haven't you?

drills.instruction: Answer the question about the modal verbs.
drills.prompt: How do the modal verbs form the Präteritum?
drills.answer: Stem **without umlaut** + **-te** + the endings of *hatte*: *können → konnte, müssen → musste, dürfen → durfte, wollen → wollte, sollen → sollte*. *mögen → mochte* (with *ch*).
drills.explanation: The forms with umlaut (*könnte, müsste, dürfte, möchte*) are Konjunktiv II and have a different meaning (*could, would have to, might, would like*).

examples.en: I couldn't come.
I could come tomorrow.

drills.prompt: Gestern ___ ich keine Lust auf Sport.
drills.answer: Gestern hatte ich keine Lust auf Sport.
drills.explanation: *Lust haben* = to feel like doing something; *Lust* is the object of *haben*. For *ich* the form is *hatte*. *war* is the wrong verb, and *hattest* is the *du*-form.

drills.prompt: ___ ihr am Wochenende in den Bergen?
drills.answer: Wart ihr am Wochenende in den Bergen?
drills.explanation: Location → *sein*; *ihr* → *wart*. *Wartet* is the present tense of *warten*, and *Waren* is for *wir* or *sie/Sie*.

drills.prompt: Nach der Reise ___ wir sehr müde.
drills.answer: Nach der Reise waren wir sehr müde.
drills.explanation: *müde* describes the subject → *sein*. *wir* → *waren* (inversion after *Nach der Reise*). *hatten* needs an object, and *wart* is the *ihr*-form.
*hatte* already contains the past marker *-te*. The *ich*-form has no further ending: *ich hatte*.
*warst* is the *du*-form. With *ihr* the Präteritum of *sein* is *wart*.

drills.prompt: Sie war nach dem Training großen Durst.
drills.answer: Sie hatte nach dem Training großen Durst.
drills.explanation: *Durst* is a noun object, and German says *Durst haben*, not *Durst sein*. For *sie* (she) the form is *hatte*.

drills.instruction: Rewrite with the Präteritum instead of the Perfekt.
drills.prompt: Ich bin letztes Jahr in Wien gewesen.
drills.answer: Ich war letztes Jahr in Wien.
drills.explanation: *bin … gewesen* becomes the one-word form *war* in position 2. The participle disappears, so nothing stands at the end after the place.

drills.instruction: Rewrite the question in the Präteritum and change *heute* to *gestern*.
drills.explanation: *hast* becomes *hattest* (*hatte-* + *-st*) and stays in position 1. The time word must change too: *heute* does not fit the past, so use *gestern*.
*die Kinder* is plural (3rd person) → *sind* becomes *waren*. The word order stays the same.

drills.instruction: Put the parts in the correct order. Start with: Gestern
drills.explanation: *Gestern* is in position 1, the verb *war* in position 2, then the subject *ich*. Without the fixed start: *Ich war gestern beim Arzt.*

drills.instruction: Put the parts in order to make a W-question.
drills.explanation: The question word *wo* comes first, the verb *wart* (for *ihr*) second, then the subject and the rest.

drills.instruction: Join the two sentences with *und*. Do not repeat the subject.
drills.prompt: Ich hatte Hunger. Ich war sehr müde.
drills.answer: Ich hatte Hunger und war sehr müde.
drills.explanation: With the same subject, *und* can join the two verbs without repeating *ich*. Each part keeps its own verb: *hatte* (object *Hunger*) and *war* (adjective *müde*).
